passage:
Before the maths exam in the school hall, Aman took out his lucky blue pencil, the one with bite marks, and tapped the desk three times. Then three more, just in case.
Gopika, at the next desk, whispered, "You know a pencil can't do sums, right?"
"I know," Aman whispered back. "But last time I forgot it and got a C."
"Last time you didn't revise."
Aman went red. "Still. I feel better with it."
Sangeeta Ma'am, walking the rows, noticed the tapping. She didn't take the pencil. She stopped by his desk and said quietly, "Lucky pencil's fine. Your revision is what does the work." Aman nodded and started on question one.

qa.q: How did Aman tap the desk before the exam?
qa.a: Three times, then three more, just in case.

qa.q: Why does Aman keep the pencil even though he knows it can't do sums?
qa.a: It makes him feel safer and calmer, and he links forgetting it with the C, even though skipping revision was the real cause.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She let him keep the harmless pencil but reminded him that revision does the work, so the ritual doesn't replace effort.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Aman's ritual?
qa.a: Gopika finds it a bit silly, and points out that the missing revision, not the pencil, explains the C.

grounding: A boy taps his desk and carries a lucky pencil into an exam, half knowing it is illogical but feeling safer with it.

passage:
My brother Sahil is ten, and he walks to school like the pavement is lava. He hops over every crack. If he steps on one by mistake, he goes back and steps on it with the other foot, "to even it out."
On match days he wears the same green T-shirt, the one with the hole at the collar. Mummy has tried to wash it twice; he gets upset.
I'm Dolma, I'm thirteen, and I once asked him if he really thinks cracks matter. He shrugged. "Probably not. But what if?"
I can't see inside his head. He does seem calmer after hopping, and he still practises batting every evening. So I've stopped teasing him.

qa.q: What does Sahil wear on match days?
qa.a: The same green T-shirt, the one with the hole at the collar.

qa.q: What does Sahil's 'Probably not. But what if?' show about his thinking?
qa.a: He half knows cracks don't matter, but the ritual still feels safer, just in case.

qa.q: When is Sahil's habit harmless, and what would make it worth talking about?
qa.a: It's harmless while he still practises batting every evening; it would be worth a gentle talk if it made him skip practice or became very upsetting.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about the unwashed T-shirt?
qa.a: A bit frustrated about washing it, but she has seen how much it matters to him.

grounding: An older sibling describes a ten-year-old brother avoiding cracks and wearing a lucky shirt while half admitting it is not logical.

passage:
Sunday. Samir laid out his lucky shirt, the checked one he wore when he won the spelling bee. "Tomorrow's science test needs it," he told Francis on the phone.
Monday. After the night's rain, the shirt was still wet on the line. Samir's stomach dropped. He wore a plain one and kept touching his collar all morning, sure he'd mess up. Francis passed him a note: "It's just a shirt. You know the stuff."
Thursday. Results came back: eighteen out of twenty. Samir stared at the paper. "Maybe it was never the shirt," he told Francis. Then, after a pause: "I'm still wearing it for the final, though."

qa.q: What score did Samir get in the science test?
qa.a: Eighteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why did Samir's stomach drop when he saw the wet shirt?
qa.a: The shirt made him feel safe, so without it he felt unprotected and sure he would mess up.

qa.q: What could Samir tell himself the next time the ritual isn't possible?
qa.a: That he scored eighteen out of twenty without it, so his own revision is what counts.

qa.q: How does Francis help Samir through Monday?
qa.a: Francis passes a note saying it's just a shirt and he knows the stuff, which is caring and down to earth.

grounding: Across a week, a boy relies on a lucky shirt, does well without it, and half admits it is not the cause while still wanting it.

passage: Raghav, before your exam, let your Hemant Dadu tell you something. When I was eleven, in our town in Satara, I had a rule. Before every test I touched the school gate three times with my left hand, then walked in without stepping on the shadow of the flagpole. Every single time. My friends laughed. I laughed too, a bit, because I knew a gate can't give marks. But the one morning I forgot, I sat in the maths test sweating, sure I'd fail. I didn't fail, by the way. I got my usual marks. Still, next time, three taps. For years. Even now, before the doctor's appointments, I sometimes tap the doorframe. So if you have your lucky pencil, keep it, beta. Just make sure you've also opened the book.

qa.q: How many times did Dadu touch the school gate before each test?
qa.a: Three times, with his left hand.

qa.q: Why did Dadu keep tapping the gate even though he knew it couldn't give marks?
qa.a: It made him feel safer and calmer before tests, and the one time he forgot, he felt anxious, so the ritual stayed.

qa.q: What balance does Dadu suggest for Raghav's lucky pencil?
qa.a: He suggests keeping the pencil for comfort but making sure he also studies, so the ritual never replaces the work.

qa.q: How might Dadu's friends have seen his gate-tapping back then?
qa.a: They laughed at it, finding it funny, though they may not have known how nervous he felt without it.

grounding: An elder recalls his childhood lucky ritual before tests, which he half knew was illogical but still felt safer doing.

passage: Exam day in Kochi, and the rain had flooded the lane. The school bus was late, and Jomon, ten, couldn't find his lucky eraser, the green one shaped like a fish. He turned his bag upside down on the floor. "Amma, it's gone. I'll fail." Seema, his mother, was holding his umbrella and the bus was honking. "Jomon, it's an eraser." "I know it's silly!" he said, voice cracking. "But I feel safer with it." Seema glanced at the clock, then at his face. She opened her own bag and pulled out a small green paper clip. "Here, borrow this one. It's green too." He looked at it, half-laughing, and put it in his pencil box. On the way, stepping over puddles, he still avoided every crack in the pavement. At school he wrote the whole paper.

qa.q: What shape was Jomon's lucky eraser?
qa.a: It was green and shaped like a fish.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he said, "I know it's silly!"
qa.a: He felt torn: embarrassed because he half knew an eraser couldn't help, yet anxious because he still felt safer with it.

qa.q: What did Seema choose to do under time pressure, and why did it help?
qa.a: She gave him a green paper clip as a stand-in, calming him quickly without mocking him, so he could get to school and write the exam.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Seema, with rain, a late bus and a missing eraser?
qa.a: It was rushed and stressful for her, but she still paused to look at Jomon's face and respond kindly.

grounding: On a rainy exam morning, a boy panics without his lucky eraser and avoids cracks, half knowing it is not logical.

passage: In the small town of Wai, the path to Ojas's school ran past the old Ganpati temple, and Ojas had rules. Never step on a crack in the temple steps. Touch the banyan three times before a test. Today was the maths half-yearly, so he hopped the cracks carefully. Kunal watched. "You know a crack can't change your marks." "I know," said Ojas, and touched the banyan. One, two, three. "Then why?" Ojas shrugged. He couldn't explain it. He had studied until ten last night; he knew the tables. But skipping the tree felt like leaving the house without shoes. "It makes my tummy feel calmer," he said at last. Kunal rolled his eyes but waited for him.

qa.q: How many times does Ojas touch the banyan before a test?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Ojas still touch the banyan even though he knows it can't change his marks?
qa.a: He feels nervous before the test, and the ritual makes him feel calmer and safer even though part of him knows it isn't logical.

qa.q: What would you tell Ojas about his banyan ritual?
qa.a: It's fine as a calming habit as long as he keeps studying, as he did until ten, so the real work stays his main preparation.

qa.q: How does Kunal see Ojas's rules?
qa.a: Kunal finds them a bit silly and rolls his eyes, but he also waits patiently, showing he accepts his friend.

grounding: Shows an older child following lucky rituals before an exam, half knowing they are not logical and still feeling safer with them.

passage: In Dublin, the morning of the under-eleven football final, Liam put on the green socks with the hole in the heel. His mum held up a clean pair. "No! These are the lucky socks. We won three games in them." He tapped the front doorframe twice on the way out, like always, and made sure to jump over the drain cover at the corner. His friend Nour, walking with him, grinned. "Do you really think socks win matches?" Liam went red. "No. Well. I don't know. I just feel better." "We won the semi because you practised headers all week." "I know." He didn't take the socks off, though. On the pitch, he wiggled his toes inside them and breathed out.

qa.q: How many games had Liam's team won in the green socks?
qa.a: Three games.

qa.q: Why did Liam go red when Nour asked about the socks?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed because part of him knew socks can't win matches, yet the ritual still made him feel better before a nervous final.

qa.q: What could Liam hold on to alongside the lucky socks?
qa.a: He could remember that his practice with headers is what really helped, and keep that up while the socks help him feel calm.

qa.q: How might Liam's mum feel about the holey lucky socks?
qa.a: She might feel amused and a little exasperated, but understand they help him feel ready.

grounding: Shows an older child wearing lucky socks and tapping the doorframe before a final, half knowing it isn't logical but feeling safer.

passage: In the exam hall of the Guwahati school, Kiran laid out his things: the blue lucky pen, which had written every good test since class five, and under his uniform, the faded cricket T-shirt he always wore for exams. He touched the pen cap to his forehead. Across the aisle, Dhruv whispered, "Still with the pen?" Kiran nodded, cheeks warm. "It's stupid, I know." The invigilator walked past and Kiran pretended to check his roll number. The truth was, he had revised three chapters twice. He knew the pen didn't know science. But when he held it, his heart slowed down. The papers came round. Kiran uncapped the pen and began to write.

qa.q: What does Kiran wear under his uniform for exams?
qa.a: The faded cricket T-shirt he always wears for exams.

qa.q: Why does Kiran hold on to the lucky pen even though he calls it stupid?
qa.a: He feels nervous before exams, and holding the pen calms his heart, even though he half knows it has nothing to do with his marks.

qa.q: How could Kiran use the ritual without depending on it?
qa.a: He could treat the pen as a calming habit and keep revising, since his real preparation, like revising three chapters twice, is what helps.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv to see Kiran's pen routine?
qa.a: Dhruv seems curious and a bit teasing, maybe familiar with the routine from earlier exams.

grounding: Shows an older child relying on a lucky pen and shirt at exams, half knowing it isn't logical yet feeling safer with them.

passage:
Monday. Kunal, eleven, had his maths exam on Friday. He wore his blue striped shirt to class every day that week. "It's lucky," he told his friend Nazia.

Wednesday. Walking to school, he avoided every crack in the pavement. Nazia laughed. "You know that doesn't do anything."

"I know," Kunal said. "But it feels better."

Friday. He tapped his desk three times before the exam started. He also knew he'd studied hard all week.

Afterwards, Nazia asked, "Was it the shirt?"

Kunal grinned. "Probably the studying. But I'm keeping the shirt."

qa.q: What did Kunal wear every day that week?
qa.a: His blue striped shirt.

qa.q: Why did Kunal keep avoiding cracks even though he knew it did nothing?
qa.a: He felt nervous about the exam, and the ritual made him feel safer and calmer.

qa.q: What would you say to Kunal about his lucky shirt?
qa.a: It's fine to keep it for comfort, as long as he keeps studying, since the studying is what really helps.

qa.q: How does Nazia see Kunal's rituals?
qa.a: Nazia finds them funny and a bit silly, but seems friendly about it.

grounding: An older child keeps a lucky shirt and avoids cracks before an exam, half knowing it isn't logical but feeling safer.

passage:
Ujjwal, you won't step on the cracks before your cricket match? Let your Saurabh dadu tell you something.

When I was ten, I had a lucky marble. Green, with a white swirl. I kept it in my pocket for every exam and every match.

One day before the school race, I lost it. I cried and said, "Now I'll lose."

My mother said, "Did the marble run the race, or did you?"

I ran anyway. I came second. Without the marble.

I still kept looking for it for weeks. I knew it didn't really help. But having it made me feel less scared. That's okay, Ujjwal. Just don't forget who does the running.

qa.q: What colour was Saurabh's lucky marble?
qa.a: Green, with a white swirl.

qa.q: Why did young Saurabh keep looking for the marble even after coming second?
qa.a: He knew it didn't really help, but having it made him feel less scared and more comforted.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Saurabh see the marble differently?
qa.a: His mother asked whether the marble or he ran the race, and then he ran without it and came second.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's mother have felt when he cried about the marble?
qa.a: His mother probably felt sympathetic but wanted to help him see his own strength.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood lucky marble he half knew didn't work but still felt safer with.

passage:
The bus to the inter-school quiz was leaving in five minutes, and Jatin, twelve, couldn't find his lucky pen.

"I can't go without it," he told his friend Shankar, emptying his bag onto the floor.

"You've got three other pens."

"Not the lucky one. I won last year with it."

"You won because you read every day."

Jatin stopped. He knew that. But his hands were shaking.

Shankar held out his own pen. "Borrow mine. It's been lucky for me."

Jatin laughed despite himself, took it, and ran for the bus. In the quiz, he forgot about the pen completely.

qa.q: How many other pens did Jatin have?
qa.a: Three other pens.

qa.q: Why did Jatin feel he couldn't go without his lucky pen?
qa.a: He felt nervous and shaky, and the pen made him feel safer, even though he knew he won because of reading.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that helped Jatin?
qa.a: He reminded Jatin he won through reading, then lent his own "lucky" pen, easing the worry with a smile.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Jatin laughs and takes the pen?
qa.a: Shankar probably feels pleased and relieved that his friend is calmer.

grounding: Under time pressure, an older child feels he can't manage without his lucky pen, half knowing it isn't logical.

passage: It was the week of the winter exams at their Lucknow school, and Kiran had a system. Left sock first. Touch the gate twice. Never step on the crack by the canteen. His friend Tushar watched him hop over the crack. "You know that doesn't change your marks, right?" Kiran shrugged, cheeks pink. "I know. Probably." He had got 18 out of 20 in maths last term on a gate-touching day. It didn't make sense, and he knew it, but skipping it made his stomach flutter. "Just in case," he said, touching the gate twice. Then he went in and read the paper carefully, the way his teacher had taught him.

qa.q: Why does Kiran keep touching the gate though he knows it doesn't work?
qa.a: Skipping it makes his stomach flutter; the ritual makes him feel safer and less anxious, even though he half knows it isn't logical.

qa.q: What keeps Kiran's ritual harmless?

passage:
"Where's my cap? Irfan, where's my blue cap?"
"Dhruv, the match starts in ten minutes, and it's forty degrees out there."
"I can't bat without it. I scored thirty in that cap."

passage: Last Navratri I had a big dance competition, and I did all my lucky things. I wore my red vest under my kurta, the one from when I won the sack race. I tapped the door frame three times. passage:
Class teacher's note, December exam week
Tushar has worn the same faded blue T-shirt under his uniform every exam day this week. On Tuesday I saw him tap his pencil box three times before starting, and he walks round the cracked tiles near the staffroom, never over them.
When I asked about the shirt, he went pink. "I know it's silly, Ma'am. It can't really help." Then, quieter: "But I feel safer in it."
I didn't tease him. I said lots of people have little rituals, and asked what else helps him feel ready. He said revising with his friend Kunal. We agreed: keep the shirt, and keep the revising.
He did well in maths. He is sure the shirt helped. I suspect Kunal did.
Afreen, Class 6 teacher

qa.q: How many times did Tushar tap his pencil box?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Tushar keep wearing the shirt if he knows it can't really help?
qa.a: It makes him feel safer and less anxious on exam days, even though he half knows it isn't logical.

qa.q: How did Afreen handle the lucky shirt?
qa.a: Without teasing: by saying many people have rituals, asking what else helps, and making sure the revising with Kunal stayed alongside the shirt.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the maths result?
qa.a: Kunal may feel quietly pleased, since their revising together probably helped more than the shirt.

grounding: Shows an older child keeping a lucky shirt and small rituals for exams, half knowing they are not logical, and still feeling safer with them.
